purpose: Provide consistent process guidance, self-check prompts, troubleshooting and mastery cues across every active Arts lesson without grading artistic taste.
principles: Guide process, observation, evidence and revision rather than aesthetic preference.
Give a clear first move so the learner is never staring at a blank page.
Explain what to notice while working, not only what to submit.
Name common mistakes without shaming the learner.
Use self-check questions before the mastery gate.
Keep no-purchase and privacy-safe alternatives visible.
Year 2 guidance should increase learner independence and professional judgment.

1.name: Creative Day
1.begin: Start with the lesson’s core creative problem. Set up only the materials you need, read the finished-task requirement once, then make the first small mark, thumbnail, test, or study before trying to solve the whole piece.
notice: What is actually present or happening—not what you assume should be there?
Which relationship matters most: proportion, value, edge, color, shape, space, rhythm, gesture, or sequence?
Where did your first attempt diverge from your intention, and what visible evidence tells you that?
common: Trying to make the first attempt look finished instead of using it as evidence.
Changing many variables at once, which makes it hard to learn from the result.
Judging the work as good/bad rather than naming a specific visual problem.
selfcheck: Can I point to one deliberate decision I made?
Can I name one visible problem and one revision I tried?
Is my evidence clear enough that I can compare this work to a later attempt?
1.mastery: Mastery is shown by completing the required creative process, documenting the work, explaining observations/revisions, and meeting the objective knowledge threshold—not by whether the artwork matches anyone’s taste.

2.name: CEO Day
2.begin: Open today’s studio/business record first. Identify the single management decision that would make the rest of the week easier, safer, cheaper, clearer, or more traceable, and handle that before adding extra administrative work.
notice: What information would future-you need to find this work, cost, file, deadline, or decision quickly?
Which bottleneck could interrupt production if it is not handled now?
What can be standardized into a reusable record instead of recreated each week?
common: Building an elaborate system that takes more time than the studio work it supports.
Recording information without naming the next action or owner.
Buying a tool when a no-cost workflow would satisfy the learning goal.
selfcheck: Could I find this record again in one minute?
Does the record show the decision, reason, date/status, and next action?
Did I reduce friction for the next studio day?
2.mastery: Mastery is clarity, completeness, traceability, and practical decision-making. Expensive tools, polished branding, or business size are never required.

3.name: Skills & Technique Day
3.begin: Treat today as a controlled experiment. Pick the exact technique named in the lesson, make a small test first, and change one variable at a time so you can tell what caused the result.
notice: What physical or visual change occurs when you alter pressure, angle, dilution, speed, layering, tool, scale, or sequence?
Which result is repeatable rather than accidental?
What does the evidence show about control, range, consistency, or limitation?
common: Practicing too large before understanding the technique.
Changing several variables at once and then guessing what caused the improvement.
Hiding failed tests instead of using them as diagnostic evidence.
selfcheck: Can I reproduce the strongest result on purpose?
Can I explain what variable I changed and what happened?
Did I preserve at least one comparison or before/after record?
3.mastery: Technique mastery means the learner can demonstrate, explain, compare, and intentionally reuse the targeted skill at the stated level—not that every mark is perfect.

4.name: Artpreneur Day
4.begin: Start from the professional asset named in the lesson. Decide who would use it, what information they would need, and what one action the asset should make easier before you design or format it.
notice: Is every required piece of information present and understandable?
Does the asset distinguish fact from estimate, draft, opinion, or future plan?
Would another person know what to do next after reading it?
common: Decorating the asset before its information is complete.
Leaving out dates, dimensions, sources, terms, costs, version information, or next actions.
Treating professionalism as expensive design instead of accurate, usable records.
selfcheck: Is the asset complete enough to use outside the lesson?
Can I identify one revision that improved clarity or reliability?
Did I save a master/editable version and a shareable/export version when appropriate?
4.mastery: Professional readiness is judged through accuracy, completeness, usability, evidence and revision. Sales, prestige, gallery acceptance, or aesthetic polish do not determine mastery.

5.name: Marketing & Promotion Day
5.begin: Choose one audience and one communication goal before making the asset. Decide what the viewer should understand, feel invited to explore, or do next; then build the smallest clear communication that serves that goal.
notice: What information is essential for the audience and what is distracting?
Does the image/text accurately represent the work without exaggerating claims?
What response would actually teach you something about clarity or audience fit?
common: Optimizing for likes or virality instead of communication quality.
Posting publicly when a private preview, mockup, or offline test would meet the learning goal.
Using vague promotional language that does not tell the audience what the work is or why it matters.
selfcheck: Can a viewer identify the work/project and intended message quickly?
Did I include a useful next step or feedback question?
Did I record meaningful response evidence rather than vanity metrics alone?
5.mastery: Marketing mastery is based on clear communication, ethical representation, audience reasoning, evidence and revision. Public posting and popularity are never required.

year2.emphasis: Year 2 moves from following a process to defending choices, comparing alternatives, documenting tradeoffs and building a coherent independent practice.
prompts: What decision would you make without a template, and what evidence supports it?
What tradeoff did you accept—time, cost, scale, material, audience, risk, clarity—and why?
How does today’s decision strengthen or challenge the larger body of work?
What would you change if this were a real client, exhibition, commission, or public-facing deliverable?

1.name: Artist Portfolio & Baseline Practice
1.mentor: Establish a truthful starting point and a repeatable evidence habit.
diagnostics: Separate observation from self-judgment.
Preserve first-attempt evidence before revision.
Use dates, file names and reflections so later growth can be compared.
stems: I notice ___ because the evidence shows ___.
My baseline is useful because it records ___ without hiding ___.
1.weakStrong: Weak: “I think it looks okay.” Strong: “The mug ellipse tilts upward on the right; I can compare that same relationship in a later drawing.”

2.name: Seeing, Contour, Proportion & Form
2.mentor: Replace symbol-drawing with measured relationships between edges, angles, intervals, negative spaces and simple forms.
diagnostics: Compare height-to-width before adding detail.
Check negative spaces as carefully as positive shapes.
Use light construction before committing to contour.
stems: The proportion changed when I compared ___ to ___.
This contour is more accurate because ___ aligns with ___.
2.weakStrong: Weak: “The object looks wrong.” Strong: “The handle begins too high relative to the rim; lowering it improves the measured relationship.”

3.name: Color Systems & Meaning
3.mentor: Use value, hue, saturation, temperature and limited palettes intentionally rather than choosing color by name alone.
diagnostics: Match value before chasing exact hue.
Compare warm/cool relationships locally.
Test mixtures in small swatches before committing.
stems: The color relationship works because ___ is warmer/cooler/lighter/darker than ___.
I reduced saturation by ___ and the result changed ___.
3.weakStrong: Weak: “I used blue for the shadow.” Strong: “The shadow is lower-value and slightly cooler than the lit plane, so I mixed the relationship rather than using a named blue.”

4.name: Composition, Hierarchy & Visual Narrative
4.mentor: Organize attention through placement, scale, contrast, rhythm, cropping and directional movement.
diagnostics: Thumbnail before enlarging.
Identify the first, second and third places the eye lands.
Check whether every element earns its space.
stems: The focal hierarchy is clearer because I changed ___.
Cropping ___ increases/decreases tension because ___.
4.weakStrong: Weak: “The composition feels better.” Strong: “Moving the dark shape off center prevents equal weighting and gives the eye a clear entry point.”

5.name: Observed Form, Light & Figure
5.mentor: Build believable form from structure, value masses, landmarks, gesture and weight rather than outlines alone.
diagnostics: Find the largest light and shadow families first.
Use structural landmarks before features.
In figure work, find line of action and weight-bearing relationships.
stems: The form turns because the value changes from ___ to ___.
The figure feels more weighted after I changed ___.
5.weakStrong: Weak: “The face looks strange.” Strong: “The eye line is too high relative to the head mass; lowering it restores the structural proportion.”

6.name: Perspective, Viewpoint & Spatial Narrative
6.mentor: Construct believable depth through horizon, convergence, overlap, scale change, atmospheric cues and intentional viewpoint.
diagnostics: Locate eye level before chasing vanishing points.
Test parallel-edge families for consistent convergence.
Use overlap and scale as checks against perspective errors.
stems: The space reads deeper because ___ converges toward ___.
Changing viewpoint from ___ to ___ changes the narrative by ___.
6.weakStrong: Weak: “Perspective is confusing.” Strong: “The table edges converge to different eye levels; aligning them to one horizon fixes the spatial contradiction.”

7.name: Composition, Rhythm & Visual Communication
7.mentor: Use repetition, variation, pacing and visual emphasis to communicate an idea across a unified image or sequence.
diagnostics: Look for repeated intervals that become monotonous.
Vary scale or spacing intentionally.
Ask whether rhythm supports the message rather than decorating it.
stems: The rhythm accelerates/slows because ___.
Variation in ___ keeps the repetition from becoming mechanical.
7.weakStrong: Weak: “I repeated shapes.” Strong: “The intervals narrow toward the focal point, so repetition also directs attention.”

8.name: Materials, Surface & Texture
8.mentor: Treat material behavior as part of meaning and technique: absorbency, layering, resistance, texture, transparency and surface preparation.
diagnostics: Test material compatibility before the final surface.
Record sequence: what went down first, what changed, what failed.
Distinguish represented texture from actual surface texture.
stems: This surface changed the mark because ___.
Layering ___ over ___ produced ___, so next time I will ___.
8.weakStrong: Weak: “I like this texture.” Strong: “Dry brush over the rough ground catches only raised fibers, creating broken light that supports the weathered subject.”

9.name: Printmaking & Reproducible Images
9.mentor: Think in matrices, reversal, editions, registration, repeatability and intentional variation.
diagnostics: Remember image reversal before cutting or transferring.
Test registration marks before the final print.
Separate accidental inconsistency from planned variation.
stems: The print changed because the matrix/pressure/ink amount ___.
This variation is intentional because ___.
9.weakStrong: Weak: “Some prints are different.” Strong: “Uneven pressure weakens the upper-right edge in three impressions; consistent baren pressure should correct it.”

10.name: Photography & Visual Evidence
10.mentor: Use photography as accurate documentation and visual communication through exposure, framing, scale reference, color neutrality and file integrity.
diagnostics: Photograph square to the work when distortion is not intended.
Check glare, focus and white balance.
Preserve an unfiltered documentation master.
stems: This photograph is reliable evidence because ___.
The crop changes interpretation by ___.
10.weakStrong: Weak: “The photo looks professional.” Strong: “The camera is parallel to the artwork, edges are visible, glare is absent, and color is close enough for comparison.”

11.name: Typography, Graphic Design & Information
11.mentor: Build hierarchy and readability through type scale, spacing, alignment, contrast and information order.
diagnostics: Read the design from six feet away and at arm’s length.
Limit competing type styles.
Align related information to shared edges or grids.
stems: The hierarchy improved when I changed ___ from ___ to ___.
This alignment groups ___ with ___ because ___.
11.weakStrong: Weak: “I made the title bigger.” Strong: “Increasing the title to the dominant scale and reducing secondary copy creates a clear first-read order.”

12.name: Art, Community & Curatorial Practice
12.mentor: Connect artwork to audience, context, interpretation, selection and responsible presentation.
diagnostics: Distinguish what the work shows from what you claim it means.
Curate by a stated criterion, not favoritism.
Consider access, attribution, consent and context.
stems: I included/excluded this work because the curatorial criterion is ___.
A viewer may read ___; the evidence in the work supporting that reading is ___.
12.weakStrong: Weak: “These are my best pieces.” Strong: “These four works share the same question about domestic space and show a visible progression in scale and material.”

13.name: Capstone, Portfolio & Artist Defense
13.mentor: Synthesize process, evidence, revision, professional records and a defensible body of work.
diagnostics: Every claim should point to an artifact, comparison or documented decision.
Edit for coherence rather than quantity.
Name limitations honestly and connect them to next steps.
stems: I can defend this decision with ___ evidence.
Across the body of work, ___ changed from ___ to ___ because ___.
13.weakStrong: Weak: “This is my strongest piece.” Strong: “I selected it because it resolves the composition problem identified in Week 10 and demonstrates controlled edge hierarchy.”

1.name: Year 2 Baseline & Seeing Beyond Symbols
1.mentor: Re-establish the baseline at a higher standard and expose habits that still substitute symbols for observation.
diagnostics: Compare Year 2 baseline evidence to Year 1 without rewriting the earlier record.
Name inherited habits that help and habits that now limit growth.
Use direct measurement when familiarity tempts you to draw a symbol.
stems: Compared with Year 1, I now ___, but I still tend to ___.
The observed evidence contradicts my symbol of ___ because ___.
1.weakStrong: Weak: “I improved a lot.” Strong: “My proportion checks are faster, but I still flatten ellipses when I stop comparing the far edge.”

2.name: Graphite, Charcoal & Ink Control
2.mentor: Develop medium-specific control and recognize that each drawing material asks for different decisions about edge, pressure, mass, permanence and revision.
diagnostics: Graphite: separate pressure from value range.
Charcoal: build mass before chasing contour.
Ink: plan economical marks because correction works differently.
stems: This medium rewards ___ because ___.
I changed pressure/mass/mark economy and the visible result was ___.
2.weakStrong: Weak: “Charcoal is messy.” Strong: “I was outlining forms; switching to broad mass first made the light pattern easier to organize.”

3.name: Paint Handling & Color Control
3.mentor: Control paint consistency, edge, opacity/transparency and observed color relationships while maintaining palette unity.
diagnostics: Test brush load before touching the developed work.
Mix enough paint to compare repeated color notes.
Judge color in relation to neighbors, not in isolation.
stems: The mixture became more accurate when I adjusted ___.
The limited palette creates unity because ___ repeats across ___.
3.weakStrong: Weak: “I need the exact color.” Strong: “The hue is close, but the value is too light; correcting value improves the observed relationship more than adding another pigment.”

4.name: Composition, Cropping & Revision
4.mentor: Use thumbnailing, cropping, scale and revision as deliberate design tools rather than rescue steps.
diagnostics: Generate alternatives before choosing one composition.
Ask what the crop removes as well as what it emphasizes.
Compare before/after versions side by side.
stems: Version B is stronger for this goal because ___.
Removing ___ increases tension/clarity by ___.
4.weakStrong: Weak: “I revised until it felt right.” Strong: “The second crop removes the competing doorway and makes the diagonal gesture the dominant movement.”

5.name: Portrait, Head & Figure
5.mentor: Unify structure, anatomy landmarks, light, gesture, character and weight without turning likeness into a beauty judgment.
diagnostics: Block head/figure masses before detail.
Check landmark relationships across the whole form.
Use light direction to clarify volume, not just decorate features.
stems: The likeness/gesture improved when I corrected ___.
This light pattern reveals the form because ___.
5.weakStrong: Weak: “The portrait does not look like them.” Strong: “The mouth is too close to the nose relative to the chin; adjusting that interval improves the structural likeness.”

6.name: Landscape, Interior & Atmosphere
6.mentor: Organize complex space through structural depth, designed viewpoint, atmospheric color and a clear sense of place.
diagnostics: Reduce the scene to major planes before detail.
Choose what the viewpoint says about the place.
Use atmospheric changes consistently with depth.
stems: Depth increases because foreground ___ contrasts with distant ___.
The chosen viewpoint makes the space feel ___ because ___.
6.weakStrong: Weak: “I added more detail to the background.” Strong: “Reducing contrast and edge sharpness in the distance prevents the background from competing with the foreground.”

7.name: Mini-Series & Midyear Exhibition
7.mentor: Move from isolated pieces to a coherent series with a visible question, selection logic and critical analysis.
diagnostics: Name the recurring question before naming the style.
Check whether each piece adds information or merely repeats.
Use exhibition order to create a reading sequence.
stems: This work belongs in the series because it advances ___ by ___.
I removed ___ because it repeats ___ without adding ___.
7.weakStrong: Weak: “They all use the same colors.” Strong: “Each piece tests enclosure versus openness through the same limited palette but different spatial structures.”

8.name: Brushwork, Edges & Material Presence
8.mentor: Treat brushwork, edge control, layering, transparency and surface as expressive systems that also need technical repeatability.
diagnostics: Separate hard, soft and lost edges by purpose.
Record layer order and drying/working conditions.
Ask whether surface effects support the subject or distract from it.
stems: I softened/lost this edge because ___.
The layer sequence ___ over ___ creates ___.
8.weakStrong: Weak: “I like visible brushstrokes.” Strong: “Visible strokes remain in the focal area, while quieter blended passages keep secondary forms from competing.”

9.name: Narrative, Symbol & Sequence
9.mentor: Build meaning through visual evidence, metaphor, context and sequence without relying on explanation alone.
diagnostics: Ask what a viewer can infer before reading the statement.
Distinguish personal symbol from culturally shared symbol.
In sequences, make each panel change information, time or viewpoint.
stems: The symbol suggests ___ because the image establishes ___.
Panel ___ changes the narrative by ___.
9.weakStrong: Weak: “This symbol means freedom to me.” Strong: “The repeated open doorway gains that reading because each panel contrasts it with increasingly confined interiors.”

10.name: Mixed Media & Experimental Systems
10.mentor: Experiment systematically across materials, processes and combinations while documenting compatibility, failure and revision.
diagnostics: Test one material interaction at a time.
Record what physically failed and why.
Choose experimental results for meaning/function, not novelty alone.
stems: The experiment failed when ___ interacted with ___; next test I will ___.
I kept this process because the material behavior supports ___.
10.weakStrong: Weak: “I tried random materials.” Strong: “Wax resisted the water-based layer and created broken edges; I repeated that effect only where fragmentation supported the subject.”

11.name: Professional Series Development
11.mentor: Define, produce, critique and unify a professional series through scope control, production planning and editorial decisions.
diagnostics: Write the series question and constraints before adding new works.
Track production status and revision needs.
Edit ruthlessly: coherence is not the same as sameness.
stems: This piece advances the series because ___.
The body becomes more coherent when I standardize/vary ___.
11.weakStrong: Weak: “I need more pieces.” Strong: “The series already has enough quantity; the gap is a work that bridges the small interior studies and the large exterior piece.”

12.name: Documentation, Statement & Exhibition Curation
12.mentor: Translate studio work into reliable professional documentation, language and exhibition decisions.
diagnostics: Photograph without distortion or uncontrolled glare.
Write statements from observable process/concerns rather than inflated claims.
Curate with explicit criteria, sequence and audience access.
stems: The statement is supported by ___ in the work.
I placed ___ before ___ because the sequence helps viewers notice ___.
12.weakStrong: Weak: “My art explores the human condition.” Strong: “These works repeatedly crop domestic thresholds to examine how private spaces signal inclusion and exclusion.”

13.name: Independent Capstone & Artist Defense
13.mentor: Operate independently: define the problem, defend decisions, present evidence, acknowledge limits and articulate the next professional step.
diagnostics: Use evidence chains: claim → artifact → comparison → conclusion.
Prepare for questions that challenge assumptions, not just praise outcomes.
Separate what you know from what you infer.
stems: My evidence for this decision is ___; an alternative interpretation is ___.
The strongest limitation is ___, and my next test would be ___.
13.weakStrong: Weak: “I chose it because it represents me.” Strong: “I chose it because it synthesizes the material layering, cropped space and narrative sequence developed across Units 8–12.”
